entry.title: The Future of AI at Rice

media:group.media:title: The Future of AI at Rice
media:group.media:description:
Rice University launched AI Week 2026 with a fireside chat focused on how artificial intelligence will shape the university’s future in research, teaching and operations. Moderated by Christopher Jermaine, chair of the department of computer science and Victor E. Cameron Professor of Computer Science, the discussion brought together President Reginald DesRoches, Howard R. Hughes Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs Amy Dittmar and Executive Vice President for Operations, Finance and Support Kelly Fox to explore the opportunities, challenges and institutional responsibilities associated with AI adoption.
The central message was clear: Rice should embrace AI as a transformative tool while preserving the human relationships, academic rigor and personalized educational experience that define the university. Rather than pursuing AI adoption for its own sake, Rice aims to use the technology thoughtfully, responsibly and in ways that advance its academic mission. Programming for AI Week includes more than 30 various panels that centered on the use of AI technology in academia. The week is a cornerstone of Rice’s WISEOwl campaign, a yearlong internal initiative supporting the responsible and effective integration of AI across campus. It bolsters Momentous, the university’s strategic plan that is shaped in part by a call for responsible AI.
Several key themes and discussion points filled the hour-long gathering.
Read more about The Future of AI at Rice in Rice News: https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/ai-fireside-chat-key-takeaways-future-ai-rice

entry.title: At the Moody, mural becomes instrument and gallery becomes stage

media:group.media:title: At the Moody, mural becomes instrument and gallery becomes stage
media:group.media:description:
Double bassist Laura Dykes and wind player Aryn Ward stepped up to a mural at Rice University’s Moody Center for the Arts and began to play it. Their Oct. 10 performance was one half of this season’s Dimensions Variable, the series of live performances and interactive experiences the Moody stages for every fall and spring exhibition. In the neighboring central gallery, Danza Azteca Macuilxochitl presented Mesoamerican dance, music and ceremony, traditions the group carries forward through lineage-based relationships with teachers in Mexico and passes between generations.
Both performances drew from “Radiant Geometries: Vectors of Knowledge from the Indigenous Americas,” an exhibition on the math, science and technology embedded in Indigenous knowledge systems. The mural Dykes and Ward played is a new commission by Diné artist Nanibah Chacon, an interactive sound installation in the Brown Foundation Gallery.
“The wavelengths emitted from this piece are permeable, an ancient technology known and practiced by our ancestors through all cultures,” Chacon said in remarks before the performance. “It is why sound is a part of prayer and capable of healing.”
Dykes and Ward of the Houston nonprofit Nameless Sound put that technology to work with an original score.
“This is something that I’ve dreamed about since creating this piece, allowing for new temporal and experimental work to be experienced,” Chacon said.
Visitors get their turn too. Chacon made the installation for anyone to play, and she said finding its meaning is up to each person who does. “Radiant Geometries” is on view through Dec. 19, and admission is free.

entry.title: Is the electric guitar cool again?

media:group.media:title: Is the electric guitar cool again?
media:group.media:description:
At 15, Chapman Welch was living a musical double life, practicing classical music while playing electric guitar for pay in bars. Those two worlds met Oct. 8-9 at the Adventurous Electric Guitar Festival, which brought guitarists, composers, technologists and students to Rice University’s Shepherd School of Music for two days of concerts, talks and workshops before closing at Dan Electro’s Guitar Bar in the Heights.
Welch, lecturer in music and electroacoustic music specialist at the Shepherd School, co-founded the festival with composer and guitarist Christopher Trapani, assistant professor of experimental music and digital media at Louisiana State University.
“Every year, a consortium of schools from Texas and Louisiana holds a student event, and as the students gather, so do the professors,” Welch said. “We started talking about a guitar festival, and because I have a lot of contacts in the guitar community, we said, ‘Let’s do an adventurous electric guitar festival.’”
LSU hosted the inaugural edition in March 2025. This year, every lecture and concert took place in Houston with support from Rice’s Creative Ventures Fund and Rice Electroacoustic Music Labs, known as REMLABS.
Erik Broess, assistant professor of musicology, opened the festival with a keynote address on the instrument’s reputation. Broess, who studies the culture of guitar tone and gear, grew up idolizing Peter Frampton, Iron Maiden and Rush, and he admitted he once felt like an outsider at a festival with “adventurous” in its name.
“Six strings on an electric guitar serve as the basis for near-infinite variation and creative reinvention,” Broess said in his keynote. “Yet the guitar is also deeply haunted by its past. Outside festivals like this one, the guitar still symbolizes 1960s and 1970s classic rock culture for many people.”
Broess traced how the instrument got its reputation. A symbol of teenage rebellion in the 1950s, Broess said the electric guitar began a long corporate slide in 1965 when CBS bought Fender for $13 million. Vintage guitars once coveted by baby boomers now sell for more than $500,000, and by the 1990s, the instrument had become background music for car and beer commercials. In the 2023 film “Barbie,” a crowd of Kens serenades uninterested Barbies with acoustic guitars around a campfire.
Read the full Rice News article: https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/electric-guitar-cool-again

entry.title: Rice launches One Giant Leap Ventures to back promising startups across university ecosystem

media:group.media:title: Rice launches One Giant Leap Ventures to back promising startups across university ecosystem
media:group.media:description:
Rice University is taking a giant leap in innovation and entrepreneurship with the launch of One Giant Leap Ventures, a new early-stage venture fund designed to invest in promising Rice-affiliated startups.
Built by Rice, for Rice, the fund will invest up to $500,000 in companies founded or led by Rice alumni, students and faculty, as well as startups built around Rice-licensed intellectual property.
One Giant Leap Ventures expands Rice’s growing innovation ecosystem by connecting entrepreneurs with institutional investment, alumni expertise, mentorship and educational opportunities. The fund supports Rice’s Momentous strategic plan and its commitment to translating groundbreaking research and ideas into real-world impact.
The fund has already made its first investment in Motif Neurotech, a Rice spinout developing minimally invasive neurostimulation technology initially focused on treatment-resistant depression.
Learn more about One Giant Leap Ventures at onegiantleap.rice.edu.

Led by Rice’s Department of Materials Science and NanoEngineering, the consortium aims to strengthen collaboration among Texas institutions through shared research resources, joint funding opportunities and expanded opportunities for students and early career researchers.

entry.title: 2 world premieres in 2 nights open Shepherd School orchestra season

media:group.media:title: 2 world premieres in 2 nights open Shepherd School orchestra season
media:group.media:description:
Two world premieres, two nights, one stage. Rice University's Shepherd School of Music opens its 2026-27 orchestral season Sept. 25-26 with back-to-back concerts in Stude Concert Hall, each showcasing a work no audience has heard before.
Miguel Harth-Bedoya, distinguished resident director of orchestras and professor of conducting, leads both programs. The Shepherd School Chamber Orchestra performs Sept. 25 and the Shepherd School Symphony Orchestra follows Sept. 26. Both concerts begin at 7:30 p.m.
Friday’s centerpiece is “Soft as the Massacre of Suns,” a set of Emily Dickinson-inspired fantasies for oboe and orchestra by American composer Jeremy Gill, commissioned by the Shepherd School and supported by the Office of Research. Erin Hannigan, professor of oboe, is the soloist in her first concerto appearance with a Shepherd School orchestra.
The premiere continues a collaboration that began decades ago at the Eastman School of Music where Hannigan was a graduate student and Gill, a composition student a few years younger, took oboe lessons from her teacher. Years later, as principal oboe of the Dallas Symphony Orchestra, Hannigan commissioned Gill’s “Serenada Concertante.”
“Jeremy always sends a letter with his composition that talks about his thinking in creating the piece,” Hannigan said. “He wrote, ‘You’ll notice this piece is completely different from the first concerto. I seem to be allergic to writing the same way twice.’”
Hannigan received the finished score in mid-June. Dickinson’s imagery, she said, gives the oboe plenty to do.
“There are some technical moments but many just gorgeously atmospheric moments where the audience should completely feel what’s going on,” Hannigan said. “There’s a movement about butterflies, and the whole movement is fluttering the entire time.”
The chamber orchestra opens the evening with Milhaud’s “Le Bœuf sur le toit,” a surrealist romp built on Brazilian dance rhythms and closes with Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5.
“Symphonic Transformations” on Saturday brings the second premiere: “Probabolophony” by Jake Berran, a 2026 Master of Music graduate in composition and winner of the Shepherd School’s 2026 Cooper Prize. Named for founding faculty member Paul Cooper, the prize is awarded annually to an orchestral thesis or dissertation and carries a performance on a Shepherd School Symphony Orchestra concert. Berran, now a Pittsburgh-based composer, pianist and conductor, has written a work that moves in and out of tonality.
The symphony orchestra surrounds it with three studies in reinvention: Ravel’s “Alborada del gracioso,” Strauss’ “Death and Transfiguration” and Hindemith’s “Symphonic Metamorphosis of Themes by Carl Maria von Weber.”
Tickets for each concert start at $5 and are available online: https://music.rice.edu/events Both performances will also be livestreamed for free: https://music.rice.edu/free-live-streams-stude-concert-hall

entry.title: Shepherd School faculty recitals reveal culture built on collaboration

media:group.media:title: Shepherd School faculty recitals reveal culture built on collaboration
media:group.media:description:
Most nights at Rice University’s Shepherd School of Music, the faculty sit in the hall and the students perform. Dozens of times each season, the arrangement reverses. A professor walks onstage at Duncan Recital Hall, usually with colleagues beside them, and the students take the seats.
Faculty recitals are a fixture of the Shepherd School calendar, and for two professors who arrived 25 years apart, they are the clearest expression of what drew them to Rice. Jon Kimura Parker, the Walter Kris Hubert Chair of Keyboards and professor of piano, has taught at Rice for more than 25 years. Erin Hannigan, professor of oboe, is in her second. Both describe the same thing: a place where artists at the top of their field make room for one another.
Parker’s first look at the Shepherd School came in 1999, on a campus tour with then-Dean Michael Hammond. Parker suspects the route that included listening in on a symphony orchestra rehearsal led by Larry Rachleff, professor emeritus of orchestral conducting, was planned.
“They were rehearsing Prokofiev, and I was blown away,” Parker said. “I thought, ‘I want to be a part of this.’”
He joined the faculty the following year. A first impression explains why someone arrives. It does not explain why a concert pianist with an international career stays for a quarter century.
“What keeps me here is the unbelievable atmosphere among the faculty and the students,” Parker said. “Every conversation I’ve ever had with a faculty member has been about what we can do to make sure the students come first.”
Parker has seen the entire student body turn over many times and colleagues come and go. But what he found in 1999 is what he finds now.
“There’s a feeling here that you can be better than you were a week ago or a year ago and that doesn’t have to come at anybody else’s expense,” Parker said.
Hannigan arrived in 2025 after nearly 25 years as principal oboe of the Dallas Symphony Orchestra. She knew the school’s reputation well before she applied, and it has held up.
“It’s a place of incredible artistry, talent and, most of all, community,” Hannigan said.
Learn more in the full Rice News article: https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/shepherd-school-faculty-recitals-reveal-culture-built-collaboration

entry.title: Rice’s Kavraki and Richards-Kortum Make History With National Academies ‘Triple Crown’

media:group.media:title: Rice’s Kavraki and Richards-Kortum Make History With National Academies ‘Triple Crown’
media:group.media:description:
Rice University faculty members Lydia Kavraki and Rebecca Richards-Kortum have made university history as the first two Rice researchers elected to all three U.S. National Academies: the National Academy of Sciences, National Academy of Engineering and National Academy of Medicine.
The rare “triple crown” distinction is held by fewer than 35 living researchers nationwide and recognizes careers spanning groundbreaking research, engineering, medicine, mentorship and service.
Rice University’s George R. Brown School of Engineering and Computing celebrated Kavraki and Richards-Kortum alongside colleagues and university leaders, honoring their contributions and the impact their work continues to have on research, education and society.
